speechtext:
I would
like to draw the attention of the government
to the condition of affairs in relation to some islands in the Georgian bay adjacent to the shores of the districts of Muskoka and Parry Sound. I understand that there have been some differences of opinion between the Dominion government and the Ontario provincial government as to jurisdiction in reference to these islands, and I would like to know whether any arrangement has been arrived at. If they are under the jurisdiction of this government I would point out that some of these islands adjacent to the township of Baxter and in that neighbourhood are assuming some considerable commercial importance. There has been a demand for these islands for summer hotel and summer residence purposes. The development of this territory is of considerable importance to some of my constituents who live [DOT] on the mainland adjacent to these islands. These people find work there and also find a market for commodities which they are in a position to supply. It is of very great importance to them that these islands should not find their way into the hands of people who will hold them for speculative purposes ; it is important to them that this district should be developed and opportunities given to those who wish to build there and develop that section of country. I think the question is of sufficient importance to justify me asking the government whether they have any settled policy with regard to the disposition of these and other islands that may be under the control of the Dominion government which are somewhat similarly situated. There should be some fixed policy and I wish to ask the government what that policy is.

Mi. A - H. BENNETT. I think it was aboiit the year 1S95 that my attention was called to these islands by a number of jier-sons who wished to become purchasers, and I at that time saw the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, or the Deputy Minister, in reference thereto. It was then decided as the minister states to withdraw all these islands from sale. I had never understood that in 1901 the then minister had made any announcement that there would be a sale of these islands either publicly or by tender, and I was rather surprised to learn later- because I live in the neighbourhood-that the government had commenced to dispose of these islands in a manner detrimental to the interests of the Indian Department which is mostly ^ interested.	To-day the minister
"ted that mJ:be case of the St. Regis reserve he would not make any sales unless with the consent of the Indians, and vet Mr. OLIVER.
liis department is selling these islands now without any consent on the part of the Indians. Grant for $140. May I ask the minister is that Mr. Grant a brother of the hon. member for North Ontario-well I may tell the minister that he is. I can tell the minister further that if this valuable island which is sold to this Mr. Grant for $140 were to be put lip tor public auction now, I have no doubt it would bring $800 or $1,000. There is about 40 acres in the portion of tile island sold to Mr. Grant, and I know that islands not nearly so advantageously situated, and also points on the mainland are being sold for $To to $100 per quarter acre. And vet here is the pmk and choice of the whole'of these islands given away to the brother of a mem-f0l' the paltry consideration of $140. Has the minister any applications in his office for this very island ?
Mr. OLI1ER. i did not make inquiry on that point ; I merely made inquiries as to the points covered by the question I would imagine that applications in the othee have been dealt with. I understand from the information given that the islands were surveyed by the surveyors mentioned and a valuation placed upon them, and that the applications for the purchase of the islands were dealt with in the order of priority and tile islands sold at the prices hxed by the surveyors when thev made the surveys.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
Had it not been for the political upset in Ontario the minister would never have been troubled about these islands, because I find from inquiries made at Toronto that this Mr. Grant and other gentlemen of the same political faith had been endeavouring to steer deals through the Crown Lands Department, but that when the political change took place in Ontario it drove them to come to Ottawa.
I am going to ask the minister :	Has the
patent issued for the grant of this lot 38 to Mr. Grant at $140 ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I cannot answer that at the moment, hut I will find out and give an answer later.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I made inquiry at the department the other day and over the signature of Mr. Pedley, I got this answer :
Letters patent have issued to Messrs James Hall Teifer and Pringle Kerr Perry for lot 38 concession 4, township of Baxter, situate on Baxter Inland, and a sale has been made to Mr. F. W. Grant of lot 38, concession 13, Baxter Island.
Might I ask the minister : Have the In- ' dians consented to these sales being made, as he stated to-day was required in the St. Regis case ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I am not aware of the facts of the matter, hut X take it for granted there must have been a general consent given by the Indians to these sales as far back as some time previous to 1884, or, the sales which have been made since that time would not have been made. I have not asked for that information, but of course I can get it. I would certainly say that the system of dealing with these islands which has been continued for 21 years may fairly be considered to be in accordance with the usual policy of considering the washes of the Indians before it was acted upon.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
The minister is unfortunate in this, that that policy was departed from, because on the remonstrance of myself and others in the year 1895, the islands were withdrawn from that process of giving them away for almost nothing. They were then advertised and bids asked for, and no one objected to that system of open sale.
I remember that several friends of mine went up there and looked over the islands, and I can tell the minister that had the islands been sold when the sale was advertised an honest price would have been obtained, because there would have been keen competition. That was in 1897 before a single hotel had been built in that neighbourhood whore there are now three or four ; before a house had been built where there are now several splendid houses, and when there was no regular boat service while to-day there is a good boat service. The minister will see that in 1897 the then minister withdrew these islands from sale and was intending to make an honest sale of them. Then came the protest of the Ontario government and in 1901 the minister announced that the policy to be followed was that persons who made prior applications would first be considered. That was fair. If a man had gone on to these islands and built a house it was only fair that he should have the first chance to tender. The minister (Mr. Oliver) cannot go back to what happened twenty years ago, because his own predecessor said in 1897 that the poliev of dealing with the islands was unfair and 'that there should be an open sale. It is also unfortunate for the minister that most of these purchases are strong political friends. D. S. Pratt, figures for island 35, I do not know what island that is and I cannot conjecture its worth. It is a rather striking thing that from the 23rd February down there have been some five grants of these islands. There was a perfect real estate business done'by this Mr. Grant who is now an applicant for this island and I regret to see that it is handed over to him. They were stopped with the Ontario government from getting these islands, and of course they had to follow down here to-Ottawa with the rest of the army of grafters. Here we have forty acres sold for $140, when I met a gentleman here yesterday who had paid at the rate of $75 for a
quarter of an acre on the mainland which in point of position was very inferior to this valuable island. Might I ask if the minister made this grant of island 38 on the 11th May ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I cannot answer at the moment; if I did I must be responsible for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Was the minister in office on the 11th May ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Certainly I was in office and acting at that time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Had the minister made inquiries of his department he would find that in 1897 the then Minister of the Interior stated that there was to be an honest sale of the islands, free from political pull and that they should be sold open and above board. Then came the conflict of authority between the local and Dominion government. Then came the principle laid down in 1901, that any person who had made a prior application for any of these islands would be entitled to the first chance of purchase. Now, I will state, and it cannot be contradicted, that this Mr. Grant had made no application in 1901, and that the minister was acting against all the precedents in his department. This is a particularly desirable island, one of the very choicest, as is borne out by the fact that here and at Toronto, I am informed from a search that was made, about half a dozen people were after this island; and from some of the names, I know that they were people who would be prepared to pay a large price for it. The minister has in his department to-day an offer of $450 for this island which he is selling for $140. I met a friend in my town a few days ago who asked me if these islands were being sold. There is a suspicion around that they are being sold in this underhanded manner, and at prices which are not fair and honest. I would ask the minister, was not application made to him personally by Mr. Grant, the hon. member for North Ontario ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I answer most unreservedly there was not. I had no knowledge of Mr. Grant in the transaction. If the sale went turough since I took office, I suppose I must be responsible for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Since the minister cannot unreservedly say whether or not the application was made to him personally by Mr. Grant, I assume that is the way it came about.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Excuse me. I said most unreservedly that there was no interview between Mr. Grant and myself in regard to this matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Nor correspondence?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
There was no correspondence between Mr. Grant and myself either

personally, toy letter or in any other way. My first knowledge of it is from what the hon. gentleman has said.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Well, the minister came into office and found that his predecessors had laid it down that there were to be no grants of sales of these islands in this manner, and yet he overrides this decision. I believe the minister has an offer for this very portion at an increased price; and yet he is selling it, in defiance of the Indian law-because I think I am within the facts when I say that there have been no surrenders on the part of the Indians of these islands. May I ask the minister finally, in regard to lot 38 on island 144, sold to F. W. Grant for $140, whether, if the patent has not been issued, he will cancel the sale, and cause this and other islands to be offered for sale publicly and above board ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I can hardly be expected to make a definite answer to a question like that on a legal point at such very short notice; but I would think that, the arrangements having been made before I took office, it would be only proper that I should carry out those arrangements. If I find that to be the correct state of the case on inquiry, I will certainly not cancel the sale to Mr. Grant.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: If that is the stand the minister is going to take, I am rather surprised. I had expected different from the hon. gentleman. When his attention is called to the fact that he has in his department to-day a letter offering three times the price for this island at which it is being sold to Mr. Grant, he proposes to carry out and consummate this deal. Whether the minister wants to accept my assurance or not, I can tell him that if these forty-five acres were put up to public sale today, I believe over $1,000 could be realized for them. It is unfortunate if the hon. gentleman should start the work of his department with actions of this kind in that part of the country. In the Public Works Department, as I said before, nobody up there expects anything straightforward, above board or honest; in the Marine and Fisheries Department it is the same; and if the Minister of the Interior is going to make a record for himself in that part of the country which will be on a par with the records of these other departments, he will pretty nearly excel the conduct of the Ontario government in regard to the Grown lands there. While there may not toe as speedy an investigation of these matters as there has been of the Crown lands affairs in that part of Ontario, I can tell the hon. gentleman, from what I have seen of some of the revelations, that they are going to be rery spicy indeed, as to how the province has been defrauded for years of its Crown timber dues, and how the Crown authorities have endeavoured to cover up the frauds.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I expected better things of the hon. gentleman; and yet he is going to hand over this island for $140 to the brother of an hon. gentleman who has already made inroads on the Department of Marine. The hon. gentleman was in the House last session when it was shown that through the influence of the hon. member for North Ontario and this very applicant, the timber on Hope Island to the value of $3,000 or $4,000 had been given away to a party friend for a paltry $100. It is true, this is perhaps not as big a steal as that was ; but I am sorry to see that the minister has no disposition to nip in the bud transactions of this kind when they are pointed out to him as plainly as this has been. His conduct will not commend itself to his political friends in that neighbourhood ; and I need not say it will not commend itself to his political opponents. I know of Liberals who are anxious to buy these islands, and all they ask is that they shall be sold openlv and above board, instead of being disposed of in the way this has been, at the cost of the general public for the benefit of some party hangers-on.
Mr. OLIVER, Mr. Speaker, if I have the privilege, I will only say that my hon. friend has taken care to leave upon the House the.impression that there have been improper transactions in connection with these lands in general, and this island in particular, and has as far as possible connected myself with these alleged improper transactions. I will not follow him in that line of argument. I merely want to place the rights of the case, as I understand them, before the House. My hon. friend has seen fit to say that the department was trespassing upon the rights of the Indians in selling these lands. That is a very serious allegation, to which I certainly would not wish to be subject; but I would point out to the House that if the department of to-day is guilty of that offence, the department" of 1S84 was the one which in the first place was guilty ccf it and continued to be guilty of it until 1896. My hon. friend will notice, in the list of sales, a series of sales which took place in March, 1896. As to the statement made by my hon. friend that a special case is made of this particular island, part of which is being sold to Mr. Grant, I do not think the .record will bear out his statement. I think the list of sales which has been placed in his hands demonstrates very clearly that his statement was absolutely and utterly unwarranted, and that there have been sales to others under similar circumstances.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Will the minister allow me to state that I find that Mr. Telfer was granted part of the same island for $240 and I would give twice as much for the part which Mr. Grant is getting.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
That is not the point I was dealing with at the moment. I hope

I shall be allowed to make my statement continuously. What I said was that the hon. member, in making the statement that Mr. Grant was being dealt with in an exceptional manner in that a sale was being made to him under circumstances under which sales were not being made to other people, was making a statement of which he had the proof to the contrary actually in his hands and under his eyes at the time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I call attention to the fact that there was another political friend, Mr. Pratt, given an island for a paltry $30.
I do not know this particular island, so that I cannot express an opinion upon it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I say the hon. gentleman is absolutely unwarranted in making the statement because he had the proof to the contrary in his hands and under his eyes. As to the method of sale, I have not been administering the department long enough to become familiar with all the details, but when I find that a certain system has been in vogue for a number of years I do not feel free to change it before making fair and reasonable inquiry. According to the memo, put into my hands, the method par-sued in selling the islands is this : A valuation was placed upon them by the surveyor at the time of the survey, and sales are being made at the price so fixed, and the applicants get the preference according to priority. That may not be the best way but it may very well be accepted as a fair way, and had it not been for exceptional circumstances, such as the establishment of summer hotels on these islands, that valuation would probably stand good to-day. But, possibly, owing to these exceptional circumstances, it has varied to such a degree as to make desirable a revaluation and a revision of the system. In 1897, the minister then administering the department made preparations for a general sale of these islands by auction. At that time the government of Ontario intervened and successfully intervened, though on what grounds my memo, does not say. The intervention of the Ontario government prevented the sale. I submit that the administrator of the department is in a somewhat difficult position. If he should wish to sell the islands by auction, there comes an objection from the government of Ontario which claims to have some right in the islands. Then when he proceeds to sell them at private sale, at the price fixed by surveyors, to applicants in order of priority, he is met with objection. I would respectfully ask what hon. gentlemen opposite suggest should be done with the islands ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

According to the memo, in my hands, the government of Ontario

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: The hon. minister should have full opportunity of making himself acquainted with this subject. I would suggest that when he comes down again, he should be prepared to answer all reasonable questions. Why is it now the policy of the department to sell these islands by private sale when up to a certain time the policy was to sell by public tender. I do not see that the intervention of the Ontario government has anything at all to do with that question. The government can come to a conclusion as to the extent to which it will regard the wishes of the province of Ontario, but surely it cannot allow that province to control it. What we are concerned with is that these islands should not be disposed of to friends of the administration at one-third or one-quarter of what other people are willing to give. That is what I would like my hon. friend to explain when bringing down further information.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I understood that the policy of the department was to put these islands up in small lots of not more than five acres. I would like to know the cause of the departure from that policy ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
The papers state that the regulation, adopted in 1887, was that the lots should not be larger than twenty

acres each ; that is if an island was larger than twenty acres, it was divided into lots and the price was fixed accordingly. Of the smaller, those islands, down to five acres, were sold separately. What I wanted to say was that, apparently, there is some claim to a right in these islands on the part of the Ontario government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

If that is the fact, of course, this department may be to blame for not having arrived at a conclusion in regard to absolute ownership- there may be some fault to be found on that ground. maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
With reference to the question asked a moment ago, Mr. OLIVER.
by the leader of the opposition as to the interest of the Ontario government in these islands, I cannot say that I can give an explanation that will be absolutely satisfactory even to myself, because I speak from recollection and it is some time since I have refreshed my memory on the subject. I believe that in this case is involved the same question that was settled in the case of the St. Catharines Milling Company. I do not know whether my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) remembers that case. It involved a conflict of jurisdiction between the Ontario government and the Dominion government as to which could sell the timber on certain lands. It was claimed by the government of Ontario because all the lands belonged to the government of the province. On the other hand, it was claimed by the government of the Dominion because this was land reserved for the Indians and the Dominion has the management of the Indians. So there will be the same case here, and that probably is the basis of the Ontario government's claim that they were the owners of the land though that land was occupied by and administered for the Indiaus.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I would suggest that there cannot be any good reason which would enable us to dispose of these lands at private sale for apparently much less than they can be disposed of at public auction, and yet would prevent us from disposing of them in the regular way.
Sir WILFRID L^uxilER. That is a part of the question. That is another aspect of the question

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) will have to inform himself on the sub-jeet. At one time these islands had very little value. If they have increased it is only of late. The Minister of the Interior will look into the matter and give an explanation. ^

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: When the Minister of the Interior brings down the papers on this subject, I hope he will include the correspondence between the Ontario government and this government in reference to the ownership of the island. I think that perhaps the same objection was made by the Ontario government as they made to the sale of certain islands of the St. Lawrence. I remember perfectly well that their objection was not that the Dominion government had not jurisdiction over the islands at all, but that, in the interest of the public of Ontario, all these islands should be reserved for common use. They made application, I remember, to the Dom-

But there is no answer to my bon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. ' Cochrane)-if you have the power to sell at all why have not you power to sell by auction as well as by any other way ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: That is the statement he made. The minister shelters himself bejiind the statement that these islands were offered at an upset price and given to applicants in the order of their application. But he must remember that the statement was made in this House by the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) that that state of affairs should no longer continue, that the public would have the right to purchase the islands by competition. That was set aside as the Minister of Interior (Mr. Oliver) says, because of any protest in the Ontario government. But since that he has exercised the power to sell without informing the House as to the altered disposition of the department in reference to these lands. We had the statement made in the House that these lands would no longer be sold by public competition. Nothing has happened since that statement was made that prevents the minister from carrying out that promise. There has been no interference of the government of Ontario that would cause or excuse any such change. The minister says that we make the sales with the consent of the Ontario government. The consent of the Ontario government would only be as to the fact of sales. If the people of Ontario have any right in these islands, their interest must be, like that of the Indian Department, that the largest sum possible should be received from the- sale of them. But, instead of that, the Minister of the Interior leaves himself open to the charge of favouritism by selling to a brother of one of the members of this House one of these islands at a price, as my hon. friend has said, only one-tenth of what should have been paid for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: If that matter is disposed of I would like to bring to the attention of the government another question-the scrip of non-resident halfbreeds. My remarks on this subject the other day were intended to bring out information and not to take a one-sided or partisan view of the matter. To-day, my remarks shall be in the same strain. I am going to ask the minister to bring down certain papers in order to show up the whole transaction, so that we may And out the facts.	,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: In a strictly non-partisan way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend (Sir U ufrid Laurier) looks rather quizzical when I make that statement ; but if he will watch, he will see that I do not go tar beyond the strictly business aspect of it to-day. My right hon. friend will remember that in 1900 or 1901, this *whole question of giving money-scrip and land-scrip to the half-breeds who had not been served before was debated in this House. That is the first point I make-that after the policy of the government was clearly stated, after objection to it by members on this side- and probably by some on the other side, though I do not remember,-and after a thorough discussion of that policy, the government's policy prevailed.
Now as a result of the conference with parliament-for that is what it was-the government got the right to dispose of a certain amount of the public domain towards the satisfaction of the claims of the half-breeds. It was upon that conference and public discussion in parliament that the first commission was appointed, of which Mr. McKenna was a x>rominent member, though I think the commission consisted of three, or four, or five, and I am quite certain there were others besides civil servants or employees of the government on it. It was a general commission. That commission went all over the ground-that is the second point I want to make-they visited the localities they conferred, after due notification was given with all and sundry who were interested, heard the evidence, made their investigation and came to their conclusions. That report was handed in in 1901, it was approved by Order in Council on the 6th of June, 1901. Now what were the principles laid down, after discussion in parliament and the revelation of the government's policy, and after that policy prevailed ? I am not going to take up every point of it, but on one point it was explicit, that with reference to certain half-breeds, those, for instance, who were not resident in Canada, who had gone to the United States and had gone upon the Indian or half-breed reservations there, and were supposed to participate in the advantages of the residence in the United States on those reservations- it was absolute in this respect that their claims were not to be allowed. I will read a summary of the report:
The claims of such half-breeds, namely, halfbreeds who were born in the Northwest Territories between the 16th of July, 1870, and the end of the year 1885, the claims of such halfbreeds were not prejudiced on account of their residence outside of the Northwest Territories, provided their parents had been permanent residents of the Northwest Territories at the time of their birth, but under clause 6 of the regulations subsequently established and approved by Order in Council of the 6th June,

1901, half-breeds who had left Canada and taken up their residence on Indian reservations in the United States and participated in the benefits of Indian life thereon, as well as all half-breed children admitted to the United States Indian schools, were excluded from participating in the grant of scrip.
That is an excerpt from the report which was approved by Order in Council. Well, now, commencing after this public avowal of the government's policy, after consulting parliament with reference to it, and after the acquiescence of parliament, the government got the right to dispose of public moneys to the amount of $240 to each half-breed, and to give scrip to the amount of 240 acres of land to each halfbreed entitled to it, to dispose of the public domain up to that amount. Now this went on for three years or thereabouts, when a change is made, and in 1904 this policy was absolutely reversed, and under the reversal of policy, the very class of claims which had been excluded, after discussion in parliament, after the investigation of the half-breed commission. after the approval of	Council-that very policy
and that very class of claims were reversed absolutely. On whose authority ? Not on the authority of parliament, not even after a consultation with parliament that it was proposed to reverse that policy. Parliament was not consulted at all in the matter ; but the minister himself, off his own bat, undertook to recommend that money and public domain which had not been authorized to be disposed of by this parliament, by conference or by acquiescence in any way, should be dispensed to a class of claims that both parliament and the government had declared should not participate in it. That is the second fact that I want lion, gentlemen to keep in their minds as we discuss it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: How did parliament declare it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I take the ground that parliament declared it in this way : That the government did what was right before they undertook to dispose of a lot of the domain of the country and of the money of the country, and they brought the matter before parliament, and we discussed it fully. Now it was an acquiescence by parliament ; whether any motion against it was moved. I do not know. If a motion against it was not moved, parliament approved of it. If there was no motion against it, then, after discussion, even though dissent was made, there was an acquiescence by parliament. It was not in the form of an enactment, because the Dominion Lands Act, I believe, is wide enough to cover even that, though I do not believe it ought to be-that is a point I will come to a little later. So I say it was really by authorization made, I am correct in saying it was with the acquiescence and assent of parlia-Mr. FOSTER.
ment at least. Now for three years that went on, when suddenly this change took place, on the initiative of the minister himself, on the 13th of August 1904. Now there might be sufficient reasons why a change should be made. There might be an agitation by those whose claims had been disallowed, thinking they had been unjustly treated, and that consequently their case should be taken up again. In the Order in Council authorizing it that is not given as a reason. It might be that friends of the half-breeds interesting themselves for the benefit of the half-breeds, would bring the matter before the government and make a plea with that old idea that the policy should be reversed and that these people should get their claims satisfied. That is not given as a reason in the Order in Council. The chief reason that is given by the minister himself is this, that it was an interference with vested interests which he did not believe ought to he any longer persisted in. Well, now, is not vested interests one of the most apparent forms of property which, from time immemorial, almost, under constitutional governments, has been discussed and is absolutely well known by governments, by members of governments and by members of parliament ? The minister himself in the very Council and in the very parliament in which this former policy was avowed and in which it was sanctioned, the very members of the government, the keenest minded of them, were there then just as they are now ; and other members of the government at that time, like Sir Oliver Mowat, like the Hon. David Mills and other men, legal men, well versed and old politicians, were there. The question of vested rights had no force in parliament in 1901, had no force in the cabinet in 1901, had no force all the time that this policy was being discussed and was being formulated and carried out. But suddenly, in August, 1904, the Minister of the Interior makes the discovery that there has been a gross abuse and violation of vested interests, and in his report to Council he recommends that this be reversed, and he opens a way by his recommendation to have all these claims taken up. Now what is the way in which he opens up the road to these claims ?	.	,
Whtn in 1900 it was proposed to give away the public domain or the public money and a commission was mooted, found favour and was adopted, it was a public commission which was appointed. Did the minister propose to appoint a public commission ! No, in the Order in Council he recommends that an officer of his department, a private employee of the department, shall have the same power that the commission had in 1900, shall traverse this question and shall take up the claims which were disallowed under that commission, investigate them and report upon them. His name is Cote and I believe he was on the former commission or

secretary of it ; I am saying nothing against him, my point is that when the minister proposes to open a way to the giving away of a large portion of the public domain or public money he does not follow the precedent in the former case but appoints an employee of his own department and obtains authority to start him on examination. It does not appear from these papers that the employee so given such powers ever advertised to the public interested that he was going to undertake another investigation, ever travelled through the portions of country where these men would be found, assembled them together, took evidence or anything of the kind. I believe from what I get from these papers that all he did was to take the disallowed claims, go over the evidence that had been submitted and make his report therefrom. It does not appear from these papers that he advertised the claimants or the holdings of meetings at which to take evidence or that he took any new evidence and then he reports, and it is on this report of his that this action is taken. The minister has not brought that report down and I do not know whether it was ever given to the minister or to the council in the shape of a formal report or whether he simply gave his conclusions to the minister and to the council, but the conclusions are all that are embodied in the papers which I have. By the former commission I think 468 claims were allowed, and 388 were rejected. Mr. Cote takes up 375 of these 388 rejected claims and his conclusions are that of those 136 are to be allowed, 09 are to be held over for further consideration and are still pending, and the remainder about 170 are to be rejected. This is the new commission, a private party, an employee of the department who without advertising, without taking new evidence, seemingly without any authorization of any public investigation so far as we can tell other than that which I have mentioned, brings in the number that I have mentioned out of the claims disallowed by the former commission and reports them as having been allowed. Now what is the next thing that takes place. So far as I can learn that, was done in August, 1904, but no notification of this was given in the ' Canada Gazette ' until October. 1904. I think it was on October 15 1904, that the Order in Council was published in the ' Canada Gazette.' The work was done in August, 1904. The resolution was confirmed, by the Order in Conn-cil in August, 1904, but no public notice of it was allowed until October 15, of the same year. That is a point which is worth while taking into consideration as well. So far as I can learn-and. I want to draw the attention of the minister to this-no notification was ever given to the half-breeds interested and no notification was given to the land agents ; there is no evidence so far as this intimation goes that the land agents were notified until March 10th. 1905. Now the most important circumstance comes in just
here. As the memorandum states, as the Order in Council states, it has been the invariable rule of the department which was embodied in a regulation and passed by Order in Council that no land scrip of these half-breeds could be located without the personal attendance of the scrip holder himself. This is a most important thing to bear in mind because with people with traits of characted such as these have, amiable in many ways, but not of the most thrifty and frugal kind, it was, I suppose, found to be the only way in which they could be safeguarded from giving up their scrip improperly, or having it taken from them improperly and so the regulation of the department, authorized and approved by Order in Council, was that there should be no assignments, no powers of attorney with reference to this land scrip, that it should not be located unless located in person by the man to whom the scrip belonged and was granted and the most stringent conditions were imposed to insure that even if his scrip were transmitted to him it should be transmitted to him in a way which would ensure its being safely carried into his very presence and given into his very hand. But shortly after the passage of this Order in Council in August, 1904, in the month of December-no I do not see that there has been any letting up of that condition which I have stated in any other way than the way that I am about to bring to the attention of the committee. The only information, the first information which comes out in these papers, is that on the 10th day of March, 1905, a departmental letter was written to the Indian agents informing them that now and from that time on this land bearing scrip could be located without the personal attendance of the person to whom it was granted.
I want the Prime Minister to pay attention to this because I think it is a grave thing for us to consider, unless other information takes away from its gravity, and I am not going to say that there is not other information to be brought down, while the invariable rule was made so by a regulation approved by Council, there does not appear to have been any approval of Council to the reversal of that rule and to the carrying out of the policy of the departmental letter written -in March, 1905. If I am correct and if this is all the information there is ifl this respect, the Minister of the Interior himself turned down the regulation made by Order in Council for the purpose of guarding the rights of the half-breed, and bv his own ministerial will reversed that policy and intimated to his land agents that personal attendance was not longer a necessity If that is so it is rather a grave matter [DOT] there may be information which would make that different and if there is we would like to have it brought down. It was an Order in Council too, that in the matter or the assignments of scrip-referring to money

scrip I suppose largely but made generally- if there was one assignment and after it another came in and then another from different parties, it was an Order in Council that the first assignment was to be the legal one. On the 17th December, 1904, the Minister of the Interior had that rescinded by Order in Council and had left the whole matter as to which of these applications should receive his assent to his own will or his own whim. It was taken out from the Order in Council which would make it go before the council ; taken out from the order which would rule him, and left entirely indefinite in his own hands. Now, I come to this other point. What reason was there why, after this policy had been settled on and carried out for three years, that in August of 1904, without a scintilla of evidence to show there was pressure by these half-breeds, the minister comes in and changes this whole policy. Why ? No pressure, no public interests, no anything ; nothing shown except the minister's scrupulous desire that vested rights should not be any longer violated as they had been. Nothing other than that his innate sense of justice and his burning indignation which after three or four years got to the bursting out point made it impossible for him any longer to sit in Council under the idea that the vested rights of these non-resident halfbreeds should not be satisfied. The uncharitable view might be, and may be a view not uncharitable, that it was the near approach of the election that stirred the^ matter. The elections were held in November, 1904 ; on August 31, 1904,'the pipe-line was commenced to be laid. What else happened ? If it is true that any notification was given to the -half-breeds'themselves who were primarily and solely interested, that their claims disallowed in 1900 bad been taken up again and were now allowed ; if there was any notification by the government or by the department to the halfbreeds, it does not appear. But it does appear that there was notification ; if not notification that information percolated to various interested persons not half-breeds : persons not interested in the welfare of the halt-breeds, not caring a bawbee for all the haif-breeds put altogether, but who belong to that class of people that are always clinging on the skirts of the government trying to find out something to get on to that they may make a penny Out of it.
XS ell they got on to it evidently, for about that time-after August and between August	and October	when the first
public	intimation of this went out
in the ' Gazette '-various things were tak-piace- A man turned up somewhere in oakota affirming that he was an agent of nL?rml0n government; having various Donnmon papers and forms about him.
a notabl? thing about it was that although he said he had come to investigate half-breed claims, the thing he wanted and Mr. FOSTER.
the only thing he tried to get was an assignment from those who formerly had rejected claims, for his own person and in his own name. I cannot do better than read an item which I find in a newspaper, which states :

hands of knowing and friendly speculators within six months of the time -that the commission sat. What is being done in these cases ? 32,640 acres of land, 240 acres for each scrip, that have to be located-for whose benefit ? The half-breeds ? Not a whit. For the benefit of the lucky one who got the information. How much has he paid for the scrip ? I do not believe on the average he has paid $100 for each certificate. Suppose he has, there are 32,640 acres of land which to-day is worth at least $6 per acre. In many sections of the country the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is not to-day selling a bit of land except to settlers at less than $6 an acre ; and the settler has to pay $5 an acre at the minimum, and $0 in a large part of the country. That land then represents a cash value of $200,000 ; and suppose that the minister, bold, audacious and unscrupulous, as he was-not my hon. friend who is sitting there, but his predecessor. My hon. friend cannot have all the honey without having some of the gall. If he takes the benefit of the office, he must take on his shoulders -the iniquities of the previous minister. If the minister, audacious and unscrupulous, as he was known to be, had come down with a proposition to take $200,000 of the people's money, and had got past the Auditor General, and had given it away to his friends, there would be something like a mild riot, though not on that side of the House. There might be some dissent on that side, but I verily believe the minister would look to his supporters to see him through. He would swear that vested rights were in question and that $200,000 was not too much to pay under the circumstances. But is it worse to take $200,000 in hard cash, unauthorized by parliament, than to take $200,000 worth of the public domain and alienate it without any parliamentary warrant ? My right hon. friend and the Minister of the Interior may plead that this is legalized by the Dominion Lands Act; but if that power is there, ought it to be exercised by a government whose duty it is to guard the public domain and the interests of this country ? That is the way the matter stands. I am not going to condemn the Minister of the Interior ; I am not going to say anything harsher than I have just said, but what I want is to get the papers down and all of them. I want the three Orders in Council which are still missing. I want that departmental letter discussed March 10, usurping the authority of the government. I want all the applications for those scrip and the lands they represent and all the correspondence in that connection, so as to ascertain what force was brought on the minister from the outside to stir him up, if he was stirred up from the outside at all. In fact I want everything concerning this transaction. If the transaction turns out to be right, the department shall have the benefit of the Mr. FOSTER.
adjudication, but it is now lying under grave suspicion. If this transaction is anything like what it is stated to be, it is time for this House and country to do a little serious thinking regarding the manner _ in which our public affairs are being carried on.

speechtext: I have made out a memo, of what I think ought to be brought down. If the minister thinks I am asking too much, let him say so. If he thinks I am not asking enough, he can supply what is wanting.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I merely make this request because on several occasions recently I have been asked off-hand for information, and the department is put at considerable disadvantage when such requests are not definite. No doubt it is the privilege of the hon. gentleman to criticise as severely as he can the conduct of the government and represent the action of any department in as unfavourable a light as possible, but in connection with this matter let me make this explanation. The first Order in Council defining the rights of the half-breeds to scrip was definite and comprehensive. ' But in giving effect to it, the commissioner saw fit to put restrictions upon the issue of scrip which had never been imposed before. There have been several issues of scrip in the Northwest. In 1885 there was an issue. Again in 1899 in the Athabaska district; again in 1900 and 1901. It was only in, 1901 that the commissioner saw fit to make this restriction debarring half-breeds, who otherwise had a right to the scrip, from participating in the grant because of their status in a foreign country. I have never been able to understand the justice of that decision. However it was given and acted upon ; but instead of the half-breeds letting the matter drop from their minds, as my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has said, they kept it very strongly in their minds. If my hon. friend knew the half-breeds as well as I do, he would know that they are a people who retain in their minds a long time a sense of injury suffered. In their opinion, the decision of the commissioner was unjust. What reason may have actuated the late Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) in moving for a new Order in Council and remedying that injustice, I am not prepared to say ; but if a substantial injustice was done, the fact that an election was approaching, was no reason why it should not be remedied. That might give grounds for the suggestion of improper motives ; but if the business of the country is to stand still because of an election, we are about to create a most re-1 markable and unwarranted condition of af-

fairs. From the standpoint of the halfbreeds at any rate and of the people of the west, who are more or less intimately acquainted with them, there was a general belief that the decision of the commission was unjust and that the remedying of that injustice was very proper. That remedy affected lands to the amount of 32,640 acres.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: That is all land scrip.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I take it for granted that it is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: In what respect was the decision of the commissioner unjust ? And why does the hon. minister differ from him ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: In my opinion, if these people had certain rights by reason of their birth, these rights were not vitiated by the fact of their removing to the United States. Until they had become citizens of the United States they still were considered as entitled to the rights they had acquired by birth. It was only such of these half-breeds as had become, in fact, through a greater or less degree, Indians of the United States that were held to have lost their rights as Northwest half-breeds.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: If I understood the minister correctly, the mere fact that they were considered Indians in the United Stated was not sufficient, but the point was that some of them had participated in the reservations set aside for the Indians of the United States, were receiving the annual grants and getting the benefit of the Indian schools. Was that not the reason ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: As I understand, it was not confined to that. Any half-breed who had placed himself, directly or indirectly, partially or wholly in the position of an Indian in the United States, was debarred. The view taken by the half-breed himself-

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I would like to get the minister's view. That view was different (from the views of the commission. I would like the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) to give reasons ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I have tried to state the reasons already, but I will repeat them. The reason why I hold a different view is the same as that which governs the opinion of the half-breed himself-that the birth of a half-breed was his title, and that his action after his removal to the United States did not in any way violate his birthright. That birthright could not be affected by his subsequent action in a foreign country. That was the view subsequently taken by the Minister of the Interior, I believe, after a full review and consideration of all the circumstances of the case-an^, I believe a just and fair view. And the Order in Council of the 13th August last, was passed in consequence of that view having been taken.
Now, again I say, the result of this Order in Council and of granting to these halfbreeds what they and a large number of the people of the west believed to be the right, has resulted or will result, in the alienation of 32,640 acres of land. Now, whatever wrong is done to the Dominion of Canada, whatever alienation of that public domain *has taken place, whatever disadvantage may accrue to this country has occurred because of this Act of, what we will say is, justice to these people, and not because of any subsequent action that has been taken. Either these half-breeds had to be refused the scrip to which they believed they were entitled as their birthright, or else that land must be alienated. There is no choice, and my hon. friend who is so very logical must take either one position or the other. That being established, I do not know that there is much more to be said. The fact that departmental instructions were issued to the land agencies to permit of entry for the land without the presence of the person to whom the scrip was issued is certainly a departure from the rule that has hitherto been allowed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Do all the minister's regulations have to be approved by Order in Council ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
Oh, yes. But this, I understand, was not a regulation, but an order of the minister to the land agent.
I am not able to answer for the minister as to the reasons for taking that action, nor am I responsible to the same degree as in the case of the Order in Council. But I take it for granted that the reasons for this permission, quoted in this case were : The non-residence of these people in Canada ; there residence at a very great distance from the office at which they must locate; their residence under the jurisdiction of a foreign country ; and, possibly, the fact that, being conuected as they were supposed to be connected, with the Indian Department of the United States, and deprived them, the privilege of removal that they would otherwise have. I cannot say what the reason was ; but I will say tills-that to have required these people to come from their residence in the United States to make their location in the land office in which they have been compelled to make it would not have relieved the country from the alienation of this land, nor would it in any way have assisted the half-breeds in holding their title to that land. It would not have inured in any way to benefit either the country or the half-breeds, it would simply have been that much money that the half-breeds would not have had in connection with the handling of his scrip. It is the half-breed, who, in one way or another, would have had to pay this cost of transportation from his residence to the
land office.	.
Now, I am not, at the moment, going

to say that it was a proper policy or that it was not a proper policy, to give this order. I am simply trying to remove the impression that was created, or attempted to be created, by the hon. member tor North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that in some way this permission resulted in injury to the halfbreeds or loss to the country. It resulted in neither injury to the half-breed nor loss to the country. There is another point to which the hon. member alluded. I think he was under a wrong impression, and I am sure he will be glad to be corrected in regard to it. In the Order in Council of the 13th of August, to which he refers, the concluding paragraph as to the assignment of scrip, is as follows :
The minister further recommends that in case of conflicting claims from assignees of such scrip, the assignee whose assignment is filed in the department first in order of time shall be held to he the legal assignee.
My information from the officials of the department is that in this paragraph, that word ' assignment ' is used in error, and that the department has never recognized assignments of land scrip.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
But of money-scrip they have ?
(Mr OLIVER. There is no assignment necessary in the' case of money-scrip, I understand ; it passes from hand to hand the same as money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Then, why was it put in the Order in Council ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I am explaining. It was not intended to be put in the Order in Council as recognizing assignments ; it was put in the Order in Council, as I am informed by the officers of the department, in mistake. The intention was to state that orders for scrip would be accepted in the order in which they came in. And the necessity for that arises from this fact-supposing an order has come in and a subsequent order comes in in regard to the same matter. The ordinary rule is that the last order cancels all the previous orders. Now the intention in inserting this paragraph was to provide that the orders should be dealt with in the order in which they came in, that the first order should be considered first, the second order next, and so on, instead of in the way such things are usually handled, namely, that the last order cancels the previous order. But the word ' assignment ' is improperly used instead of the word ' order.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: If that is so, of course it explains the matter in hand, but it is not an endorsement of the efficiency of the departmental officers and of the minister himself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
Now to prove what I say that there was in some sense an error, I may say that under that paragraph, which evidently contemplated assignments of scrip, Mr. OLIVER.
there have been no assignments recognized. It was in force from the 5th of November, 1904, until the publication of the cancellation in February, 1905, but during that time no assignments were accepted. The cancellation took place in September, but the publication was not made until some time afterwards. It was cancelled in December because it was recognized as being an error. If the hon. member will give me a memo, of the papers he requires I will be glad to have them brought down if possible.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I would ask the minister if he is aware of the fact that there are a number of half-breeds in the Northwest at the present moment who think they have not been justly dealt with, and who think they still have claims for scrip or land. In the section where I live, there are quite a number of people with such claims. They went before the commission, but they think they were not properly dealt with in some way, that their representations were not given due weight, that their claims were rejected without proper consideration. I believe that they expect even yet that a commission will go up again and take up these unsettled claims. During the winter I have received several requests to bring this matter before the government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I could not give an answer to that question at the moment, but I take it for granted that if It shall be shown that substantial injustice has been done, an effort will be made to remedy that injustice. But I do not think there is any probability that a new issue1 of half-breed scrip will be made on any other terms than issues have already been made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
Of course there are reasons I suppose, set out in these Orders in Council-which I have not had an opportunity to examine very carefully-upon which is founded the decision of the department to set apart by means of this scrip a certain amount of the public domain of this country for half-breeds residing in the United States and proposing to make the United Stakes their permanent place of abode. Unless there is something in the statutes or in the compact of by-gone days which makes that necessary, I would not think it a very desirable policy. I would think it far better to restrict the allotment to such of the half-breeds of the United States as propose to return to this country to take up their permanent residence ; otherwise I think that it might not he an unfair mode of dealing with the subject, to take those portions of the public domain which otherwise would have gone to these men who have left this country and gone to the United States, and allot them to such as have chosen to remain in Canada and make this country their home. Under the statement of facts made by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), it looks as if it were not so much the interest of the half-breeds that

was being regarded as tbe interest of friends of this government ; and that after all, probably not 10 per cent of the land, at least, which has been allotted under this arrangement ever benefited the halfbreeds in any respect whatever ; and I would infer from the facts laid before this House, that at least nine-tenths of it have gone to the comfort and sustenance of certain gentlemen who happen to be very close in touch with one or more departments of this government, and who have been enabled, by means of this arrangement undertaken in tbe month of August last on the eve of a general election, very considerably to improve their financial condition. However, we will have the rest of the papers down, and we will have a discussion on the subject. This seems to me to belong to the same class of cases as the wire fence case we discussed the other day, the fishing privileges which were mentioned not long ago, the islands in the Georgian bay which have been discussed this afternoon, and the bitulithic pavement contract which was also mentioned in this House a few days ago. These all seem to be very much in the same category. But of course, as the minister is not yet very familiar with his department, and as he has not yet been able to ascertain exactly what the House demands, it is only right that he should have an opportunity of bringing down the papers, when we shall make any criticism which may be called for by the additional information.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I would ask the minister in this connection as to whether the Nixon papers are approaching completion ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: They are ready, I have been negligent in bringing them down.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I wish to refer a moment to the sale of islands in the Georgian bay.
I think the minister should be able to give to the House a statement of the policy of hi.s department in future as to the sale of islands not only in the Georgian bay but in other parts of Canada. When this government came into power they put an advertisement in the papers offering to sell 1,000 islands in the Georgian bay, by public tender. I have a copy of the advertisement in my hand, bearing date, Ottawa, 16 July, 1897. Tenders were received up to noon of the 2nd day of August in that year, for about 1.000 islands situate in the Georgian bay. Without reading the whole of the advertisement, it says :
The highest or any tender *will not necessarily he accepted.
For myself I wish to say that I do not think this is the best mode of selling islands in this country at the present time. While it may be thought better to sell them by tender rather than to sell them by private sale, yet I am of opinion that the proper way to sell islands and other parts of the public domain is by public auction. I think the 207	.
minister should make it clear to the House this afternoon that, whatever the policy has been in the past, for the future no islands will be disposed of in the Georgian bay district except they are weli advertised in different newspapers in this country, and a day fixed so that every man may have an opportunity of coming in and giving his highest price. A survey was made of these islands in 1896

Surveys of the islands in question were made by Mr. Charles E. Fitton, Ontario Land Surveyor, Orillia, and Mr. J. G. Sing, Ontario Land Surveyor, Meaford, under instructions given them on the 4th and 17th of June, 1896.
This advertisement was published asking for tenders, and a protest was entered by the Ontario government, showing that the latter did not agree with that policy, and therefore no sale was made. But the matter was revived in 1901, and from 1901 down to the present time several sales have been made. Since this parliament has been in session, five sales have been made to friends of the government, one sale on the 23rd of February, 1905, to Robert Wood, for 8105 ; another sale on the 23rd of February to S. G'rozelle, for $45 ; another made on the 25th of March to Emma Poole, for $20 ; another on the 12th of April to A. W. Mitchell, for $50 ; another on the 11th of May to F. W. Grant, for $140.
My hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) who is familiar with the island purchased by Mr. T. W. Grant, a brother of the sitting member in this House for North Ontario, who is well acquainted with that section of the country and is conversant with its values has made the statement this afternoon that if that island had been sold by public competition it would have brought in the neighbourhood of $1,000 to the treasury of this country instead of $140 when sold to a political supporter for $140. If those five islands that I have referred to had been put up for sale by public competition and the value of the other four were equal to the value of the one referred to by the hon. member for East Simcoe, then instead of $360 being found in the treasury for these five islands, the sum of $2,160 would have been paid into the treasury and every man in this country would have been satisfied were he a supporter of the government or a supporter of the opposition. I do not wish to enter into a further discussion now as some other .papers are to be brought down. I wish to direct my remarks for a moment to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior. While we do not wish to hold him altogether responsible for the sins of his predecessor in office yet my hon. friend has- had due notice of this question because the hon. member for East Simcoe wnote him on May 18, saying that he wished to bring this matter up at the first opportunity. My hon. friend has since that date had this matter under his consid-



eration. The hon. member for East Simcoe objected and said that in his opinion the sales should be made by public competition and now that this matter is before the minister, before the House and before the country as well-because the country takes a very deep interest in this matter and there have been charges from every province in Canada, and particularly from the province of Ontario against this government that there are certain public domains being sold to political supporters of the government in power-I thought my hon. friend would be anxious to clear the government of that condemnation if it is possible for them to clear themselves, and therefore I ask the minister if he is prepared this afternoon, and if not this afternoon if he will be prepared within a few days, to make a statement to the House that hereafter no islands in the Georgian bay district will be offered for sale by private tender or sold to a political supporter, but that every island in future shall be advertised and sold by public auction at a fixed date that may be advertised to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: If I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, I do not know that it is perhaps well to use the time of the country at the expense which is entailed by the sitting of parliament, in the discussion at very much greater length of the sale of these islands. The hon. member for Pee] has suggested a hope that I will later on make a statement according to the suggestion that he makes. Let me point out that while on one hand that may be a good suggestion in the administration of these lands, on the other hand it may not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Hear, hear, for the boys.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: There are there, islands I understand, varying in size from an acre or less up to thirty or forty acres. They are not, if I understand the matter aright, of any value agriculturally, but they are valuable as summer resorts to put it mildly. Now while one or two or a few of those islands may be especially valuable as sites for summer resorts, I think everybody will admit that there is not a demand for a'thousand valuable summer resorts on the shores of the Georgian bay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: You try a sale.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I am suggesting the idea that if some person comes along and wishes to build a cottage upon an island in the Georgian bay that has an area of an acre, and the soil of which is as nearly pure rock as it can be, then if the country is compelled to go to the expense of advertising the sale of that island, hiring an auctioneer and selling it by auction, the system will be open to very grave objections from the point of view of the man who wants to buy an island to build a cot- I

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: tage on. The attempt of the government in 1897 was to sell all the islands at a single auction or rather by tender.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: One or more?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I understood it was to sell them all. They were all offered for sale.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: The advertisement was read and the minister said no tender will necessarily be accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Surely all advertisements read in that way.	.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: That is one of the chief objections, that the highest or any tender may not necessarily be accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: All government advertisements asking for tenders for supplies of any kind say that the lowest or any tender shall not necessarily be accepted and I presume the same rule is quite as applicable in the case of islands that the highest or any tender shall not necessarily be accepted because the tender may not be high enough to warrant the government in disposing of the island. That is a saving clause that must necessarily be inserted if the public interest is to be protected. I know I am not justified in taking up time to point out these details to the House, but I think since so much has been said it may be worth while considering whether there shall be an invariable rule of advertising and selling by auction every island for wicli an application may be made. Let me briefly sketch the facts of the case. The islands were surveyed and they were valued by the surveyors. This schedule and these prices, as I understand, were available to applicants for the islands. Applications have been dealt with in the order in which they were made and I submit that however improvident the action of the government or whatever loss may have resulted to the country by their adopting that principle the charge of political favouritism does not lie against the government if that is the system and it has been followed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: In 1897, the hon. gentleman's predecessor laid it down that the highest bidder would get them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I think the hon. member will not say for an instant that the government should advertise a sale of islands and say that the highest bidder should get them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
Not if you want your friends to get them. It is all they have left now, it is their only graft.
Some hon. members. Order, order.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I think I have fairly pointed out that there is no graft in this transaction.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Try a sale and see.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Tlie arrangement has been open and above board ; and if it is a fact that owing to the circumstance of the increased value of some of these islands the revenue of the Indians is suffering, that of course is a matter to be fairly taken into consideration and some arrangement possibly made, but I submit that the fact that one or two islands may have achieved a value of $140 or $400 is not sufficient ground under the circumstances of these various sales to make a charge of political favouritism. 1 will go so far as to say that I do not think that in this country or any other country, a man is to be debarred from ordinary business transactions because he happens to be related to a member of parliament who happens to be supporting the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Nobody contends that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I may say that since these islands began to be sold, since the question of the Indian rights in the islands was settled by the action of the government in 1884, there have been altogether 104 islands sold. Prior to July, 1S96, 69 sales were made of islands, or parts of islands, of a total area of 1,012'.'10 acres, and the price realized was $1,846.95. Subsequent to July, 1896, 35 islands have been sold, with a total area of 438-74 acres, and the price realized was $3,002.75.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: You would not compare the value of the islands fifteen years ago with their value to-day ?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I am only giving the facts ;
I am not making any comparison. Of these islands which have been sold since July, 1890, seven were sold for the benefit of the Indians to the Marine Department for sites for lighthouses or other marine improvements, with an area of 189-60 acres and at the price of $1,377.75. I submit that the facts and figures do not show that this government has been negligent of the interests of the Indians.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
