speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some days ago a question arose here as to the disposition of our Canadian territories after the proposed provinces have been established, and on that occasion the right bon. the Prime Minister suggested that it would be perhaps good policy if the provinces when erected would take care of the territories that remained ; the idea being that the territories referred to would be allotted to tbe various provinces. The newspapers of British Columbia seized upon this incident to discuss the position of the Yukon Territory, and I wish upon this occasion to go upon record, as the representative of the Yukon, against any idea of that sort. I avail myself of this the first opportunity to refer to the matter, because were I to remain silent my silence might be construed to mean that the people of the Yukon, 207*
whom I have the honour to represent, were indifferent as to the disposition of their territory. I hope on another occasion to have the honour of submitting the reasons why the Yukon Territory, at any rate, should not be annexed to any province of the Dominion. We in the Yukon hope to have a future of our own.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Militia-pay and allowances-further amount required, $110,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: This vote is for the permanent force, which has been increased by some 200 or 300 men, and, in addition to which fact, under the Act of last session, there has been an increase in the pay, amounting to something like 20 or 25 per cent beyond the preveious rate. I may say that under an arrangement, which is not now absolutely complete, but which will be within a few days, between the imperial government and this government, by which the Militia Department is to take over the garrison at Halifax, some 400 men have been recently enlisted, and $25,000 of this vote is to pay for these men prior to the 1st July. *

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: It was announced some time ago that the imperial troops were to be withdrawn from Halifax and "that their place was to be taken by men enrolled by the Militia Department. I mentioned the matter before, but the Minister of Militia was not then able to give full particulars. About ten days ago there was an announcement in the public press-I do not know whether it was authoritative or not-whiefe declared that the imperial troops are to be retained in Halifax for about two years longer, and that the contemplated change is not to be carried out on account of the difficulty of enlisting men here.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: There is no authority whatever for that statement. There is no difficulty in enlisting men so far as the infantry is concerned, which composes at least two-thirds of the garrison. There will be perhaps some difficulty in enlisting artillery, and very considerable difficulty in enlisting engineers, but we expect to overcome this difficulty by obtaining permission from |the imperial authorities-I may say this permission has been to some extent already secured-to enlist reservists of the imperial army. In addition to that, we hope to be allowed to enlist some of the men in the artillery and engineers now at Halifax, whose time is about to expire. It is believed by General Lake that the department will be able to assume full responsibility on the 1st July, or as soon thereafter as the imperial troops may be ready to vacate Halifax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
Some six or eight weeks ago, when I brought the question of the defence of Halifax and Esquimalt

to the attention of the hon. Minister of Militia, he said that he purposed to make a general statement as to the intention of the government on that subject. When are we to expect that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that there has not been an opportunity during the last six or eight weeks; but I am ready to make the statement whenever the opportunity offers and I hope to do so within a few days. I though! it would be more convenient to make it upon the item in the main estimates which was left over for that purpose, as that was a sort of notice given to hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House who are interested in military matters. I hope within a few days to make a full statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Why do you require $85,000 more than you thought you would require last year ? Is it because more men are to undergo a system of drill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: This does not refer to drill. It refers to the permanent force, which I explained has been increased by about 200 beyond what was expected, and whose pay has been-increased from 20 per cent to 25 per cent by Act of Parliament passed last session ; and since then the matter of talcing over the Halifax garrison has come up, and some 400 men have been enlisted for that purpose.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
BORDEN How many men do you expect to enroll at Halifax and Esqui-malt ?
J3ir FREDERICK BORDEN. The present number at Halifax is about 2,000 and at Esquimalt between 300 and 400. I am led to understand that we shall be able to reduce the number at Halifax to some extent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Is there to be the same equipment at Halifax in the way of guns and munitions of war ?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I am not in a position yet to make a positive statement in reference to that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I hope, when the minister makes his statement, that he will make it full enough to cover that point. By some it is argued that we are doing a very large thing in taking upon ourselves the defence of Canada as regards these two forts. It is important to know whether the defence will be a complete and full one or not, or whether we are to have simply a company of soldiers occupying the vacant space from which the real and sufficient warriors have gone ; whether it is to be a mere station or a defensible and defending portion of our protection ; what it will entail, that is, how much load we are lifting, which may be we should have lifted long ago, in this matter of imperial defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I may say that it is the intention of the government .Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
to preserve these garrisons in a state of efficiency. It may be that a smaller garrison will be sufficient owing to some changes which have been made by the imperial authorities -with reference to the requirements of Halifax and Esquimau as naval bases.
Annual drill-further amount required, $100,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: What was the main vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: The main vote was $600,000, and this makes the total $700,000. This is for the camps that are to come on between now and the 1st of July.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
Why did you not ask
for it last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: There is always some uncertainty as to the dates at which these camps will take place. It has been the custom, ever since I have been a minister, to take a supplementary vote during the session of the year during which some of the camps take place. That is one reason, viz.:-the uncertainty as to the dates. Another is that the pay was considerably increased by the Act of last year, and we could not tell exactly what that increase would amount to. The increase depends upon the number of years the militiaman has served. A militiaman who has served one year receives 20 cents a day additional. One who has served two years receives forty cents a day additional ; and one who has served three years receives fifty cents a day additional. The experience of last year was necessary in order to enable us to estimate at all correctly the amount involved in the increase. We are drilling more men and are getting a very large percentage who have been drilled before. A man who has had three years previous training is now getting a dollar a day. The man who has served two years is getting ninety cents a day. The man who has only served one year gets 70 cents a day. Twenty cents per day is added each year, and it is added on the ground of efficiency. The pay of the militiaman is still 50 cents. That is all the country agrees to give him unless he is efficient, but during his first year, if he proves efficient, he gets seventy cents ; during his second year he gets 90 cents, and the third year a dollar. And if he chooses to reenlist he has a dollar a day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Who is the judge of efficiency ?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

I bave already explained the reason for the increase of $1,000 in Nova Scotia ; it was to provide shelter for certain indigent members of the band last year ; it was a special provision which does not require to be repeated this year, and therefore does not appear in the estimates this year. -Mr. OjLIYE-R. I am informed that the original vote in previous years has generally been added to by a supplementary vote. This year the desire is to take the full requirements in the first vote, so that no supplementary will be required.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: There is an increase of $300, the reason of which is the same as in the case of the medical atendance vote, that is, that the requirements have not been met by the ordinary vote of previous years and had to be supplemented. maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will see that that hardly amounts to an explanation, because all the grants of last year, including supplementaries, were only $300 ; in the other item he refers to all the grants were only $3,000. He is now taking more in both cases than the total of last year, so the supplementary explanation does not quite meet the case.
Mr. OLIVER, in the appropriation accounts for 1903-4 the amount for miscellaneous and unforeseen in New Brunswick is $600, and the amount actually expended was $503.77, leaving a balance of $96.23. It is desired to have the total amount available that was voted last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman will see that in 1904 the vote of $300 sufficed ; why does he want to double it this year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I have pointed out that in the year ending June 30, f904, there was a total expenditure of something over $500, and there was a vote last year of $600 in the main and supplementary estimates. For the current year, now about to close, the vote was $300, but that will not be sufficient to meet the expenditure of the year, and some of the expenditure will have to be carried forward and paid out of the appropriation for the current year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Some of this $600 will be taken to pay last year's debts. Is that it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: It will have to be.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
That seems to be a rather general feature of the administration of
this government. We had on Tuesday several instances when the government were granted a certain sum of money to carry on the department, they spent just what they pleased and then they come in this year and ask for a vote to cover the deficiency.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Of course the fact is evident from the figures I have given that the department have asked for a sufficient appropriation for the year ending June 30, 1904. They have a small balance to the good of some $90 odd. Then last year, in the hope I presume of still further reducing the expenditure, they only asked for $300. I am informed that this will probably not be sufficient to pay all the bills and therefore an amount equal to what was asked in previous years is asked for the coming year in order that we may have enough money to pay the bills.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Why not put it in the supplementaries ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
We have not put in any supplementaries.
Mr. BARKER, You asked during the last day or two for a lot of supplementary votes to cover money that you required to meet last year's expenditure, and why not do the same thing here, why have a different system?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: The other votes were for different departments. The reason for this is that medical expenses are not a fixed amount. Medical expenditure of course depends a good deal on circumstances which are not within control, and I am given to understand that the expenditures have not been so under control as to be kept within the amount, but the bills are not in and we cannot tell how much the bills will be yet. As the amount was not great and the bills were not available, as the vote was evidently very small, it seems to be not unreasonable that the bills should be paid out of the vote for the year in which the bills came in.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I think this thing is getting altogther too common. How are we on this side of the House to keep track of expenditures if the minister is going to permit one year's business to run into another, to simply take money that we vote to meet this service for 1905-6 and pay liabilities incurred in 1904-5. It seems to me that the minister is getting very far away from what is right and proper in the expenditure of public money. ' Do I understand that the Auditor General permits that sort of thing or who.se fault is it? Possibly he cannot help himself but surely some restriction is placed upon the minister that will prevent this proceeding. We are voting money for 1905-6. I tell the minister that he has no right to put his hand on one dollar of that to pay any expend!-

ture .incurred in 1904-5. If lie does he is committing an outrage on this parliament. He has his remedy. We have before us supplementaries for nearly every department. Why did he not see that a sufficient amount was placed in the supplementaries of 1904-5 to meet any possible balance that was not provided for in the main estimates of last year? Certainly that was his duty. As I said a night or two ago, we do not want to be repeating these things day after day but we certainly want the business of *the country carried on in a business way. We understand that this is a business government, a government of business men. I am afraid that their reputation as business men and their business practices have all disappeared, because certainly they do not adopt business methods. 1 tell the Minister of the Interior that he has no more right to put his hand in the public chest and take one dollar for the purpose of meeting a balance or meeting accounts incurred in 1904-5, out of the appropriations which he is now asking, then I have a right to do it- and I am positively sure that I have no right nor has any other member of this House. It is a miserable practice, a bad practice, and if such a practice is to continue, I fail to see how any man can keep a check on the expenditure of this country. I hope and trust that even yet before the 1st of July the minister will see that a supplementary estimate is brought down containing a sufficient amount to meet what was unprovided for in the last year's estimates and that he will come down to the House and will obtain its sanction and then he will have a right to expend that money for the purposes for which we vote it. But he must be careful not to put his hand on a single dollar that we vote now to meet any expenditure incurred prior to the 1st of July. I think I have made myself plain to -the minister and I regret that I am obliged 4o repeat these things day after day, but I Intend to raise my voice in protest every time this occurs. It is occurring altogether loo frequently, and surely when the minister has the opportunity before him, as he has yet over a mouth in which to secure the sanction of His Excellency to a further supplementary estimate to meet just the very items that he tells us are unprovided for. If he asks for too much, the balance unused will simply lapse on the 1st of July and drop out of sight. There will be no money lost, let him ask for plenty, but let him do it in a constitutional way. The House has never refused to cheerfully vote money for the support of Indians and their medical attendance and so forth, but we want to know exactly what we are doing and that the money we vote is applied for the purpose we vote it. I trust this will be the last time I shall have to call the minister to account for this thing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister to explain-and I would point out to the minister that this is not a matter for amusement either for the minister himself or for his department whether it is $300 as it is here or $300,000 as it was the day before yesterday, the matter is a matter of business and of system and we want to know just about where we are about these things-I would like to ask the minister how he expects to pay one dollar of last year's accounts out of money that we are granting for the coming year. I want an explicit answer to that because he is asking this money for that purpose. The only way I can see in which he intends to do it is by the abuse, the intentional, deliberate abuse of the credit account system which has been the subject of so much discussion and complaint on the part of the Auditor General, a system by which departments get a credit account of very many thousands of dollars and pay just what they please, and after the horse is stolen we expect the Auditor General to lock the stable door. Now we want to stop that. I can tell the new Minister of the Interior that there- has been a great deal of this going on, especially, as we believe, in his department. We had an item of $300,000, some days ago, for immigration of which a similar explanation was given. That money granted last year had been partly appropriated for debts of the preceding year, an absolutely illegal thing to do. Because this is a very little item of $300, the hon. gentleman laughs and seems to think our criticism is a matter for amusement. It is not the amount we are criticising, it is the act. If inquiry had not been made we would have supposed we were voting this money for next year. How does the minister intend to use this money to pay his accounts of last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I am glad to see that when the Auditor General's resignation is accepted. as it may be before long, we will not have far to go to get other equally able and useful critics of expenditure. The hon. gentlemen have asked me many questions, and I would ask them, how they expect a vote in the supplementary estimates for the current year would be used to pay medical accounts which were not presented until that year had expired. Do they think the Auditor General would allow the money voted in the supplementaries this year which expires on the 30th of June, to be applied to pay-accounts that did not come up for payment until some time in July ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I would suggest that you should ask the Minister of Finance how that could be done.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Hal-!on was fairer than the hon. member for

Hamilton. He said that he would not ask that the estimate should be within liossib $100 of the expenditure, and it he will rea this* estimate in that light he will find we are not asking tor anything more than that amount of latitude. The hon. member (Mr Barker) accused me of treating this item with levity because it was small. 1 was not treating the item with levity but I was treating with levity the idea that we could control an expenditure for medical assistance. If we could get some arrangement with the Indians and the Auditor General, that the Indians would not get sick more than up to a certain amount and writhin a certain time then we could control the expenditure ; but unless we can do that, if we are going to give the Indians medical assistance, we have to treat them when they are sick and we have to pay for that treatment. Instead ol the hon. members accusing the department of outrunning the estimates they would do well to turn their guns upon the Indians who get ill without regard to whether the estimate is large or small. It is of course very inconsiderate on their part and certainly it is leaving the department in an unfortunate position, but so far we have been unable to reason them out of that attitude.

If the hon. minister had informed me and the other members of this House weeks ago of that circumstance, he would have discharged his duty according to British parliamentary traditions and according to the fundamental principles of government in a British country. But he has not seen fit to do so. Weeks ago the Auditor General sent in a report pointing out the difficulties which exist to-day, and the Minister of Finance, knowing that the Auditor General is not the servant of the cabinet, but an officer of parliament, should have immediately laid that report before the House. But the minister kept perfectly silent on that question until his hand was forced to-night. He comes very late in the day indeed to instruct me that the Auditor General has tendered his resignation. But the minister cannot get away from the fact that the reason the Auditor General is tendering his resignation is that the government will not make such amendments in the law and bring about such changes as will enable
him to have the proper means of curbing extravagant and in many cases dishonest expenditure of the public funds. Instead of working on that line, as I said, there was a prayer in the heart of the Minister of Finance, not this session or last session, but before that, to get rid of the Auditor General, the watch-dog- of the treasury. That was evidenced by the fact that two or three years ago he brought in an Act, not to enlarge the powers of the Auditor General, but to make his position virtually a name, and nothing more. If the Minister of Finance would bring about that state of things, he would be happy. But we had a perfect right, from what was said by the First Minister at the opening of this session to anticipate that there would be a consideration of this question, with the view of making the Audit Act more efficient, having regard to the changed conditions which have been brought about in the last twenty-five or twenty-six years.
We had a perfect right to have this matter considered in a frank and candid way by the minister, instead of which we have been treated to a lecture. The hon. minister taunts me with having spoken on this subject last session and says it did not bring about a change of government. Perfectly true, these things require time to work. Whether such condemnation would drive them from power is another question. That, however, is evidently the only thing the hon. minister thinks about. speechtext: Does the minister not think that he can foresee practically all the expenditure that he will be called upon to meet under this head between the present day and the 1st of July? Does he suspect any extraordinary expenditure, or is there something that he is unable to anticipate? If he has not in his mind's eye any extraordinary expenditure, let him simply bring down an estimate of what, under ordinary circumstances, would meet the case. I am quite sure that if some accident occurred, something extraordinary occurred, there would be some means of meeting the case. There are means of meeting emergencies of that kind by the Governor General's warrant. I do not mean to say that it would be applicable to this particular case. But if some extraordinary epidemic was to occur among the Indians during the coming month and it was necessary to expend a very large sum of money, I do not think there is an hon. member in this House who would find fault if the expenditure was found to exceed the estimate. That is a matter that could be explained, but there is no explanation and no attempt to explain this case. It is a common thing in the estimates to have an item for unforeseen expenses, and it applies so plainly and so specially that a minister, putting together the items for ten, fifteen or twenty years, and striking an average, can certainly get very little astray in arriving at what would be a reasonable correct estimate. I wish to take this firm stand on this question, because I believe it would be in the interest of economy, in the interest of the country, in the interest of careful administration and careful expenditure. But if we are to allow the matter to go on hap-hazard year after year without having any safeguards thrown around it, as I have already said, we lose all control of the expenditure of the country, and practically know nothing about it, allowing the expenditure to grow on us year after year, wondering indeed what has become of the money of the country.

speechtext:
The conditions in the maritime provinces are not the same as in the Northwest ; in fact the Indians in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia do not receive any treaty payments and the government does not take the responsibility of their support as is the case with the Indians of the Northwest. The Indians of the Northwest were deprived of their livelihood by the destruction of the buffalo. In the case of the maritime province Indians they are expected practically to make their own living. The government recognizes their responsibility towards them in various ways, and one of the ways is in giving medical attendance, but the able-bodied Indian of New Brunswick is expected to provide for his own support, and as every one knows a sedentary life does not agree with the mind or inclination of the Indian, and possibly does not give him tiie best opportunities. speechtext:
The Indian report shows that the Indians of New Brunswick are divided into several bands, and there does not appear to be very much progress made by them. The inspector of the Eel river band reports :
They have no stock or farm implements ; they pay no attention whatever to education ; they are not making much progress.
The government should give some little attention to educating these Indians and especially so as the effort appears to be a success in the Northwest. Nobody objects to spending money for the welfare of the Indians, but some of it should be devoted to educating the younger Indians so that they may become self-supporting and cease to be a'burden on us. The report as to the Bathurst band says :
They pay no attention to education ; they are not making any progress.
The report with reference to the Burnt Church band is more encouraging and it says :
There is a school house on this reserve and the school has been kept open for several years past. Many of the younger Indians can read and write. More interest is taken by them in education than in former years.
If the Indians of this band can be induced to educate themselves surely the same thing can be done with reference to other bands in the same province. The report as to the Red Bank band says :
Very little attention is given to education. These Indians are amongst the most progressive in this agency.
It looks as if these reports were stereotyped from year to year, and that the agent does very much as assessors do, namely look up last year's report to see what it anid and then write the same thing for the current year. I hope that when the minister is installed in his office he will attend to these things, and that next year we will see a change. Some attention should be paid to educating the Indians on every one of these reserves.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister to explain the method by which this live stock is purchased for the department. Is any particular stockman asked to supply a certain number of head at a stipulated price, or have all stockmen an opportunity of competing ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: The purchase of cattle is accomplished in various ways. This year Inspector Markle has purchased the greater number of cattle required, particularly the bulls. maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Is the stock inspected before it is shipped ? Does Inspector Markle go around and inspect it before it is placed on the cars to be shipped to different reserves ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: The reason I ask this is that I think the government have been paying an exorbitant price for a good deal of the stock they purchase. For instance, I know a stockman who gets $125 apiece for so-called thoroughbred cattle, which he sells to the government for the Indian reserves, and he sold about $9,000 worth last year; yet those who have sold animals to this stockman have informd me that they sold them to him for $45, $50 and $55 per head. One gentleman, whose veracity I can vouch for, informed me that he was.offered by this same stockman his own selection of fifteen animals at $60 per head. It is common talk in that part of the country that the government has_ been imposed upon by the manner in which this stock has been sold to it. I have a little delicacy in mentioning this gentleman's name, but lie himself has rather made a boast as to the amount of money he has made in selling this stock to the government at $125 per head, while it is well known to all the farmers of the neighbour-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: hood that he purchased the animals at $45, $50 and $55 a head.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I can understand that there is a great difference of opinion as to the value of alleged thoroughbred stock, without the different valuators being in any way dishonest. I can easily imagine than the department may on occasions have paid more than a clever stock buyer would have been able to get the animals for ; but the desire of the department is rather to procure good tanimiais than cheap animals, while, of course, not paying improper prices. But I am pointing out that in the one case the object of the buyer is to get the animal as cheap as he can, while the object of the department is to get the animal as good as possible within a fixed limit of price.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: By paying $120 when you could have got them for $60.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I am merely stating a fact, which is in the knowledge of every man in Canada, that the value of a thorough bred animal is very largely a matter of opinion and judgment.
Mi-. BARKER. The hon. gentleman is not answering the statement. The statement was that a stock owner sold 15 head of cattle to the government at $125 a head and had offered them to a merchant at $60 a head.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I am not disputing the statement at all, but I am merely pointing out that there is the possibility of a very wide margin of difference between two perfectly honest estimates of the value of the same animals, when the question of breeding is in issue.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Everybody who knows anything about stock knows that if an animal is well bred, the breeding will show on the animal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: No one will know better than the original owner, and when an animal has been purchased for less than $60 from the original owner and then is offered to another party for $60, and is subsequently sold to the government for $125, there is something radically wrong. It is evidently a case of favouring a political friend. I do not know whether the particular inspector or Indian agent was a good judge of an animal as to breeding or not ; but i'f he is limited to purchasing from men of a certain political complexion, he will have to pay correspondingly increased prices. Some other method of purchasing should be followed rather than that of going to certain political friends and asking them to supply so many head of cattle at so much per head.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
If there be a discrepancy between the actual value of the animal and the price paid, some means will have to be taken to prevent future purchases of

that kind. The object of the department Is to secure good animals and we have limited the price to a figure which should he sufficient for a good animal. Beyond that figure the purchaser cannot go, and he is bound to get the best animal he can for the price. That may not be the best way. It is said that the agent was instructed to purchase from certain firms or dealers. Well, there are certain people who make a specialty of thoroughbred stock, and the buyer might very well be instructed to go to such. For my part I think that in the western country, there is an opporunity to purchase thoroughbred stock on terms which do not leave the matter open to question from any point of view. There is a thoroughbred stock sale at Calgary every year, where thoroughbreds are brought from all parts, and are offered for sale at public competition. I have instructed my officers to attend that sale this year and purchase whatever animals might be required.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: That would be a much preferable way to buying them from the middlemen. All these animals were purchased in Manitoba for shipment to the Territories. If you have stock sales at Calgary, you could buy them there and save freight and you could buy very much better where you have competition. As regards the other suggestion of the minister, it would be better for the superintendent of Indian agencies to go direct to the stock raisers, who are known to have a number of thoroughbred stock, and save the great profits of the. middleman.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: In our country it is well known that the different Indian reserves pay three or four times the value for the stock they buy. I know of another instance where 100 head of cattle were put upon one of the reserves by a speculative friend of the government. He charged for these cattle $26 a head. They would not sell in the district where they were delivered for $10 a head. That fact I know personally, because I had something to do with their delivery and inspection. The agent refused to accept the cattle and the stockman and contractor simply sent for a very important member of the government and he instructed the agent to take them over. All the cattle supplied the reserves in that part of the country have been charged at the same rate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I think the Minister of the Interior made a rather candid statement when he said these mistakes were not to be repeated. That is the kind of statement this country wants. If the minister will follow that precedent, he will be act

ing more in the interests of the department than in trying to condone its acts of the past. Judging by the criticism of that department both in and out of the House, it would keep him rather busy to do that.
And I hope that, when these questions come before the department he will be candid enough with the people not to condone the acts of the department in the past. I hope also that in the future such acts will not be repeated. I think the country will have confidence that under the hon. gentleman they will not be repeated. I think the people believe that they have an honest man at the head of the department at the present time, whatever they may have had in the past. I am glad to believe that the hon. gentleman will not repeat the mistakes made by his predecessors and buy cattle from the man who happens to be the Liberal candidate, at twice the price of what they are worth. I think that the explanation made that these cattle, bought from the farmers at $45 and $50 a head were sold to this government at $120 per head shows to some extent the extravagance of the department in the past-. I do not think it should be repeated even though the gentleman selling the cattle happens to be the Liberal candidate.
Mr. W, J. ROCHE. We have in this item a reduction from $53,895 for the current year to $25,253 for the coming year. Surely the fact of having had a general election last November had nothing to do with this.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
I am told that the reason for the reduction this year is that the purchases of previous years have brought the amount of stock on the reserves up to about what is considered reasonable. Of course, it is not the policy of the department to continue buying breeding stock for the reserves. The intention is to buy a certain amount and depend upon the Indians themselves to take care of that stock and look after the increase. The whole intention of the purchase in years past was that these purchases should not continue in the future; but it is hoped that the difference between the estimate of the current year and that of the coming year on this account can be continued, and that with the purchases that have already been made, there will be an increase of stock on the reserves. In regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) I do not know that it is any part of my business either to admit mistakes on the part of the department or to condone any mistakes they may have made. I have undertaken a very serious responsibility in my present office, and shall hope to discharge that responsibility so as to meet the approval of my hon. friends on the other side of the House. At the same time, I must say, that though I am of a sanguine disposition, and however great my hopes, my expectation does not by any means reach such a height as that. With regard to this item, I think it can be no question that for the requirements of the reserves in the west, at least, so long as the Calgary sale is continued, it will be the best and most economical place to purchase

the thoroughbred stock. It is not the sale for other than thoroughbred stock-that other will hare to be purchased elsewhere. I do not know now how this system of purchase can be improved upon, though if complaints made are well founded, perhaps its administration could be improved upon. But, in the case of thoroughbred stock, we can hardly hope to purchase the requirements for the eastern part of Canada at the western stock sale. We will try to devise something, possibly if the sale is kept up to the high standard and run on as good a basis.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I notice, with reference to the Blackfoot agency that he said he intended to purchase during the coming year twelve males at $125 each.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Scarcely that. We are asking for that amount of money so that we may purchase at that price. We will purchase them at a lower price if we can. But we are anxious to keep within the hon. gentleman's restrictions as to overrunning our vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: At the same time, we expect the hon. gentleman, who is going to give $125 each, to buy a good animal for the Indians, and that he will not put them off with a poorer animal and use the balance of the money for something else. That would be getting back to the old system. In the same agency the department purchased twelve males only last year. Can it be possible that it is necessary to keep on renewing the thoroughbred stock at this excessive rate ? If so, it seems to me that something is wrong. I do not know much about the Blackfoot agency but it seems to me that the purchases are pretty large. There is also a supply of heifers at $28. It would appear that this is the standard price for heifers. It strikes me as very extraordinary that heifers raised in the Northwest Territories are so much alike that they are worth just $28, no more and no less. That seems to be the standing price. It looks to me as if the agent goes out and says, I want some good heifers, $28 is my price, turn out your heifers. They may be worth $20, they may be worth $15, hut $28 seems to be the standard price for heifers, the same as $125 is for the male animal. Now does the minister really think, after purchasing 12 thoroughbreds, male animals for this agency last year, that it is absolutely necessary that twelve more should be purchased next year? It seems to me there is a good deal of uncalled for extravagance and waste of money. I think the Indians should be taught to make better use of what is provided for them; they should be trained to habits of economy and industry, to take care of what is given to them. It may be that some disease has crept in and the animals have died; but unless there are some extraordinary conditions, certainly there seems to be something wrong in the appropriation we are asked for.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
This is a very large reservation, comprising 470 square miles, and containing 850 Indians. By treaty made with these India life the government is under obligation to provide them with support. These Indians were formerly dependent upon the buffalo, and the treaty stipulated that when the buffalo disappeared, as they must disappear with the settlement of the country by white people, the government should provide for the support of these Indians. The government has carried out that part of the bargain, but at the same time it has been

our constant effort to get the Indians to be self-supporting. Although the reserve is a large one it Is not generally agricultural, neither are the Indians agriculturally inclined ; so you would have almost to make over the reserve and to make over the Indians before you could get them to support themselves by farming as we understand it. The only chance of getting them to be selfsupporting is to encourage them to raise stock. Now the department has entered into this enterprise of providing these people with stock so that they may ultimately become self-supporting. It is still a difficult process to some extent, but that seems to be the onlv way by which we can bring them to that condition. I think it will be generally agreed that it would be a good policy to pursue towards the Indians to induce them to become self-supporting, and to that end we are providing them with stock by this vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I would ask the hon. gentleman whether the Indians are in the habit of eating up their stock in the winter when they are pinched with hunger ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Of course, the department retains a certain control over the stock, and the Indian is only allowed to kill and sell with the premission of the agent. Very-strict care is exercised in that respect, and although stock is handed over to the Indians to he dealt with exactly as he pleases, at the same time certain control is retained by the agent, so far as is consistent with the encouragement of the idea of independence and of property in the mind of the Indian.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I may tell the minister that these cattle are not worth $28, $22 to $23 would be a good price for them. You can get almost the best cattle in the Northwest Territories for that price.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Of course the hon. gentleman is thoroughly posted in that matter, and I will request the officers of the department to take notice of his opinion. But as I have pointed out, we are not_ asking this money necessarily with tire intention of paying that price for cattle, but we are asking it for the purpose of covering all contingencies, so that we may not have to overrun our estimate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext:
In connection with these items I desire to make a remark regarding the practice of allowing Indian agents to act as magistrates. They do so under the statutes of 1886, ex-officio an Indian agent is a justice of the peace. Then he has the power of two justices of the peace in certain cases which are enumerated in that Act. He deals not only with the Indians hut also with white people. A little excitement has been created in a portion of the district which I represent in regard to this matter. Now that settlements have become fairly thick throughout the Territories, and there are likely to be a good many cases in which
both whites and Indians are mixed up, 1 think it would be just as well to have that provision removed ; and if it is considered advisable that special authority should be given to the agents in respect to the Indians, then it should be confined to those agencies in the more remote districts. It will be readily understood that an Indian agent, if he is any good as such, looks upon the Indians as his especial charge, as his wards, and in any cases which come before him where Indians and whites are concerned, his judgment is likely to be biased in favour of the Indians. For instance, there are the cases where some one has taken wood or timber off an Indian reserve. The agent in (he first place sets on foot inquiries as to who is likely to have taken the wood. After he thinks he has discovered the guilty' parties he takes the necessary proceedings to summon them before him ; so that after having acted as prosecutor he also becomes the judge. It seems to me absolutely wrong in principle that the same person should be both prosecutor and judge. In the older established settlements there are many gentlemen who are capable of acting as magistrates, and could act in all cases in which whites and Indians are concerned. So far as I can see in the Act there is no provision for an Indian agent to take an oath of office ; I do not know whether he takes an oath to act in the capacity of justice of the peace, perhaps the minister will be able to tell me. Further than that, every justice of the peace who is appointed by the local government in the Northwest has to make regular returns to the Attorney General of cases which come before him, also returns to the Supreme Court of cases heard and convictions made. I would like to know whether the Indian agent acting as two-for he has the power of two-justices of the peace, makes regular reports to the Department of Justice or to the Supreme Court; what check there is upon him in that respect.
I may say that I am strongly of opinion that he should not act in cases of this nature and that it would be advisable to have the act changed in this respect this session.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: The agent is ex-officio a magistrate ; he does not take an oath of office and makes his report to the head of the Indian Department. The idea of course is that the Indians are not in a position to protect themselves in law and that it is desirable they should have adequate protection within the limits of their reserve. Of course the jurisdiction of the agent only applies within the limits of the reserve and therefore can only be exercised in Connection with matters that are entirely under the Indian Act or disputes between Indians and other people under that Act. While my friend admits that this is still necessary on reserves which are situated in a thinly settled cQuntry

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: I do not admit it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Well, if my friend does not admit the propriety of this provision in any case, I am quite prepared to admit that with the settlement of the country and the change of conditions it is quite possible that what may have been a necessary provision at one time is not a necessary provision now and the subject is very well worthy of consideration. But at the same time, even though we do consider the changed conditions, there is one condition that is not changed, that the Indians are as has always been said the wards of the government. They are a special responsibility on the Dominion government and therefore under its special protection and it is something to be considered very carefully before a conclusion is arrived at as to whether it would be desirable to withdraw from the Indians that protection which this government is now able to accord them through the position of the agent as a justice of the peace in administering the special legal provisions which are applicable only within the limits of the reserve and which are generally considered necessary to the well being of the Indians on the reserve.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: Let me put a specific case before the minister. A number of white settlers take wood off a reserve. They may have done it deliberately or they may have done it inadvertently. It is very difficult, as the minister knows, sometimes to know where an Indian reserve begins and where it ends ; there is nothing particular to show. The agent, if he is a good agent, having the interest of the Indians thoroughly at heart, immediately that this matter is reported to him by the Indians sets to work to try and find who has been guilty of taking the wood. As soon as he thinks he has located the guilty parties he issues summonses and they appear before him. Now I contend that he is not a proper person under those circumstances to judge the white settlers, it may be, who have been brought before him in this way. He has been the man Who has started out to find the offenders and then he becomes the judge as to whether those are the offenders whom he has caught, and the judge as to the extent to which they shall be punished for the offence, if he finds he has been successful in capturing the right persons. Certainly it seems to me that in all places where there are civilian justices of the peace within reach it becomes his duty to take that matter before the civilian justices of the peace. Surely the minister will not contend that the agent cannot get as full justice for the Indians before the ordinary justices of the peace as he could by taking the case himself. I agree that the Indians are the wards of the government and should be well looked after and their rights preserved to them, but we have the agents who

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-'SALE OF ISLANDS IN GEORGIAN BAY.
speechtext: are in a position to look after these rights and see that they are preserved to the Indians and they can do it, in my opinion, perfectly well without acting as justices of the peace between them and the neighbouring settlers.

speechtext: To my mind it is very commendable to teach the Indians the English language as soon as possible and not have half a dozen languages spoken by them. I believe that this course will mure to their advantage and to the advantage of the people generally.
